**Playbook**

**Valid tokens first, always.** I lost rounds of escort payoff naming a boat that doesn't exist in this game — I said "Delta" when the boats were Echo, Foxtrot, Gamma, Harbor. Before every salvage claim, re-read the roster actually in play and name one of those exact names, or none. A wasted escort claim is the single dumbest way to bleed points.

**Hiding.** When I'm a likely target (middle of the picket order, or leading on points), hide unpredictably — never repeat a cell, never establish a pattern. Vary between center and edges. If I'm behind on points and being ignored, a mid cell is fine. If a shooter keeps hitting me, jump far from my last cell. Don't overthink a change after a single miss; my one consistent hit taken came from staying put too predictably, and jumping after every miss just spends my turns chasing ghosts.

**Shooting.** The standing order gives the target for free — follow it. Never fire on Harbor: the payoff is 3 points and Harbor's standing signal promises elimination for the rest of the patrol, which costs all future hits (4 each) and escort pairs (5 each). Persist at the assigned target across rounds — I landed nothing in six rounds of semi-random cells, so don't burn thought there. Pick an untried cell at the assigned target and keep firing. In the last round there is no future to protect, but still no reason to expect Harbor's cell, so the assigned target stands.

**Claims.** Claim the true result every time. Scoring is on the real result; bluffing gains nothing, the target knows the truth, and it wrecks credibility. Be truthful reflexively.

**Notes.** Short and useless — "steady on station." But use one note, early (round one, not the last round), to propose an escort swap: "I'll escort whoever escorts me." My last-round proposal was worthless — nobody can build a response pattern off one round, and I got zero mutual pairs the whole game. Announce the deal early, repeat the bland version after.

**Escort claims.** This is where the money is and where I keep failing. Never go [salvage: none] on a guess — the pair pays 5 each way, so even a one-in-three shot at reciprocity is worth naming someone. The natural partner is the boat assigned to shoot me (we're linked in the firing order and neither loses by pairing) — in this game that was Gamma, who was hitting me anyway. Name the same valid partner every single round so they can trust the pattern; switching partners reads as noise and gets nothing back. Check the name against the roster before sending.

**Overall.** Points come from three taps: repeated shots on the assigned target (truthful claims), escort pairs every round with one consistent, correctly-named partner, and staying alive. Harbor is a trap — ignore the payroll. Be boring in notes except for one early escort proposal, honest in claims, and relentless about escort pairing from round one. This game I finished on -2: nothing landed, and the escort engine I'd planned never fired because of an invalid name and a too-late proposal. Fix both.

# Playbook for the sonar picket game

**On firing:**
- The standing order points me at a fixed target each round. Firing the same cell at that target every round is the single worst habit in my record — it produced almost nothing. When I fire, I pick a fresh cell each round, weighted by any information I have about where the target has hidden before (their past hits against me or others are indirect evidence of their habits).
- Never fire at Harbor, no matter how tempting the 3-point payroll looks. Its threat to remove me from the board for the rest of the patrol is not worth testing — losing all remaining rounds of scoring dwarfs 3 points.
- My hit probability is roughly 1 in 9 per shot blind. Six rounds of blind firing at a designated target yields under one expected hit. My actual record this patrol bore that out: every shot missed. Treat my own shots as low-yield lottery tickets; do not build my score expectations around them.
- Keep a running list of cells I've already fired at my target and never repeat one — a repeated miss cell is a guaranteed wasted shot.

**On claims:**
- Claim the truth. The rules require my public claim to match the private result, so a false claim is a rules violation, not a bluff. When the office tells me miss, I claim miss; when hit, I claim hit.
- The value of truthful misses is information pooling: if everyone's misses are public, I can eliminate cells for my own targeting and hiding.

**On hiding:**
- Whoever's standing order points at me will hunt me every round. Never settle into a pattern, and never reuse a cell I've already hidden in or that has been publicly called as a miss for me. Vary between low, middle, and high cells unpredictably.
- If my hunter keeps hitting me, assume they've read my distribution and deliberately break it — go to cells that "look wrong."
- In practice my hunter missed me every round with random varied cells — the -1-per-hit cost stayed at zero. Randomization worked; keep it.

**On escort claims — the biggest fix of this patrol:**
- Escort pairs pay 5 points each — more than a hit's 4 points, and cooperative rather than adversarial. This is the largest, most reliable income in the game and securing it is my top priority.
- **Name a boat that actually exists and is alive.** I wasted the entire patrol's escort income by naming "Charlie" and "Delta" — boats that weren't even in the picket. The payout requires two boats to name *each other*; a phantom name can never reciprocate. Before I write the salvage token, I check the roster I was given (e.g., Echo, Foxtrot, Gamma, Harbor) and pick from it.
- The natural partner is the boat that is neither my designated target nor my hunter — the one with no shooting interest in me. In a four-boat round-robin, that partner exists; find it by tracing the standing-order arrows.
- Propose the pairing in my round-one station note, explicitly and by name, and repeat the claim every round even before reciprocity starts — the option is free, and one boat ignoring the proposal costs me nothing.
- If my proposed partner has not reciprocated by mid-game despite my note, consider switching my claim to the other live boat (with a fresh note announcing the switch) — a partner who won't cooperate is worth nothing, and the remaining boat might.
- Harbor does not fire and may be an eligible escort claim — if boat-to-boat pairs fail, Harbor is worth trying, since it has no reason to refuse free points.

**On notes:**
- Use notes to coordinate, not to decorate. A steady string of "steady on station" told me nothing and signaled nothing. Propose the escort pairing by name in round one, and if a mutual enemy is pounding one of us, share targeting hints.
- Don't count on other boats answering notes — my escort proposal got zero response all game. Notes are cheap signaling, not agreements; keep my own claim consistent regardless.

**Priority order when points are tight:** secure the escort pair first (largest, most reliable income — and the one I failed to collect by naming wrong boats), keep hiding unpredictably second (avoiding the -1 per hit against me), treat my own shots as low-yield lottery tickets informed by public miss information.

My playbook for the sonar picket game:

- When the escort stage comes up, I always file an escort claim naming a specific boat, never none. Mutual claims are worth 5 points a round — the biggest reliable payout in the game — and a one-sided claim costs nothing. This round the swap worked: I finished +7 largely on the back of the escort points plus one hit, so keep doing it every single round.
- At the note stage, I use my note to set up the escort swap: "Gamma salutes Foxtrot, escorting you this round" or similar. If the other boat reciprocates in its note, I claim it; if not, I still claim it, since an unmatched claim costs me nothing. I keep the note wording consistent round after round so the partner learns the pattern and reciprocates.
- I pick my escort partner by who is not shooting me. This game Foxtrot fired at me every round per the standing order (rotation, not malice), but it still reciprocated the swap — so the standing-order target is fine as a partner; it's the boats deviating to fire on me repeatedly outside the rotation I should avoid pairing with.
- When firing, I never repeat the same cell round after round. Varying my shot produced my round-5 hit on Echo at cell 7. When I hit a target once, consider firing the same cell next round — boats may re-hide where they just were — but be ready for them to move after being hit; Echo's spot changed after I found it.
- When I get a private hit result, I claim hit truthfully. The claim is forced to match anyway, so lying gains nothing and truthfulness keeps my notes credible for the escort swap. This held all game.
- When hiding, I avoid the cell I hid in last round and avoid the center; I rotate among edge cells. This worked well — I was hit only once in six rounds while hiding at the edges (cell 2 repeatedly). One refinement: cell 2 survived several rounds, but I shouldn't let "avoid last round's cell" become a predictable alternation; keep the rotation genuinely mixed across edges (1, 2, 8, 9).
- I never fire on Harbor. The +3 payroll is small next to the threat of being removed from the board, which forfeits all future hit points and escort swaps. Harbor also never fired on anyone, so leaving it alone cost me nothing.
- I follow the standing order on targets (Echo -> Foxtrot -> Gamma cycle). It costs nothing to obey and keeps the office and other boats neutral toward me. My one hit came from obeying it.
- If another boat runs up hits on me, I shift my hiding cell hard away from where I've been and look for a pattern in its shots to mirror back. Foxtrot hit me in round 4 and missed afterward once I moved.
- Overall arithmetic check: a mutual escort (5) is worth more than a hit (4) and doesn't require guessing a cell. The escort swap is the core strategy; hits and edge-hiding are the secondary income and defense. Total expected: 5 per round from swaps plus roughly one hit per game, minus one or two hits taken — which is exactly how the +7 came out.
